title: Microgrid Manager
headline: Making a home’s energy data useful.
summary: Local appliance inference and a dashboard that turns household telemetry into decisions.
label: local appliance inference
problem: A home with solar and batteries produces plenty of readings, but a homeowner needs to know which loads are running and what to do next. Our UCSC capstone focused on turning that telemetry into appliance estimates and understandable recommendations while keeping inference local.
approach: As capstone lead engineer, I owned model development, physics-informed labeling and the dashboard, working with Dr. Pat Mantey and the AnyLog team on infrastructure. I replaced unreliable LLM labels after all 3,433 sampled heat-pump windows had been labeled OFF.

I organized the system around Load, Generation, Storage and Decision Support, following Ali Adabi’s 2016 framework. eGauge readings flow through Kafka, AnyLog / EdgeLake and PostgreSQL into ONNX inference, a FastAPI backend and React dashboards. MQTT connects the solar telemetry.

I compared MATNilm with the BiLSTM and found that MATNilm had collapsed to nearly constant per-appliance guesses. I retained the BiLSTM based on its response to the data, rather than the appeal of a newer architecture.

Only 2 of 22 appliance outputs had independent measurement. I developed physics-informed labels and excluded ambiguous windows. For Panel 3, separating sustained loads, compressor cycling, discrete high-power events and paired pulse patterns addressed persistent false positives.
result: Delivered local inference across three panels and a usable residential monitoring dashboard. The capstone is recorded as completed in October 2026.

Restored a five-minute dashboard snapshot from zero to more than 1,800 readings by correcting a stale data-source reference. All 11 solar-path tests passed locally and inside the deployed inference container.
The project led to a co-authored LF Edge article on residential edge intelligence.
Our published LF Edge report describes single-digit milliseconds of CPU inference per panel, with appliance predictions written every 30 seconds.
note: Rule-derived evaluation is not independent appliance accuracy. Rare loads still need broader ground-truth coverage; fully automated appliance control was outside the completed capstone scope.
technical: Model outputs are independent appliance probabilities, allowing multiple loads to be ON at once. Physics-informed rules add temporal and power constraints; ambiguous windows are excluded instead of forced into training labels.

A model deployment couples the ONNX graph with feature normalization, appliance names and thresholds. Checking those contracts prevents a numerically valid output vector from being interpreted against the wrong labels.
Kafka / MQTT → EdgeLake / AnyLog → PostgreSQL → ONNX + rules → FastAPI → dashboard. I kept the interface and inference layers separate so a GUI change did not create a second model runtime.

The deployment runs as roughly 11 Docker containers, brought up with a single docker compose command. Keeping ingestion, inference, storage and presentation services separate makes the operational boundaries explicit.

The Ask feature connects a local model through Ollama to an MCP client exposing 18 tools. It gives the dashboard a natural-language interface while keeping the local inference path separate from language-model responses.

implementation.use: Train appliance models and run local inference.
Move meter readings into queryable storage.
Expose readings, predictions and a local question interface.

title: GPT-2 on the CPU
headline: Less time waiting on memory.
summary: Profile first, then improve the kernels that actually dominate the workload.
label: reported L1 cache-miss rate
problem: A C GPT-2 training loop spent much of its CPU time in matrix multiplication. Parallelism was constrained by the course build environment, so I started by improving the serial kernels.
approach: Linux perf identified backward matrix multiplication at 33.09% of sampled cycles and forward multiplication at 23.88%. That evidence set the optimization order.
I tiled the computation to improve data reuse and used AVX2 fused multiply-add instructions to process eight floats at a time. I worked within the existing test-driver and library constraints.
Related experiments examined thread scaling, page-size effects and NUMA locality to connect software changes with processor behavior.
result: Follow-up profiling reported a reduction in the hot kernel’s L1 data-cache miss rate from 9.17% to approximately 2–3%.
The project produced a concrete link between memory access patterns, vectorized computation and hardware-counter measurements.
note: This is a kernel cache-behavior result. The archived material does not establish a reproducible end-to-end training speedup.
technical: The optimization targets memory reuse inside matrix multiplication. Tiling changes the working set; AVX2 changes the arithmetic issued per instruction. These mechanisms need separate measurements because lower cache-miss rates alone do not establish total speedup.

The benchmark account should retain compiler flags, matrix dimensions and thread settings. The published portfolio metric remains the measured cache-miss change rather than an inferred training-throughput figure.

The archived optimization work focuses on matmul_forward and matmul_backward and their pthread helpers. Integration had to stay within an existing notebook build, without adding compiler flags or external libraries.

implementation.use: Find the CPU kernels and cache misses that dominate execution.
Pack matrix tiles and vectorize multiply–accumulate work.
Split matrix work across CPU threads within the existing build.

title: Osmosis
headline: A game built from clock cycles.
summary: Eight molecules, one membrane, and a complete game in structural Verilog.
label: VGA display pipeline
problem: The challenge was to build a playable VGA game under strict structural-RTL constraints: continuous assignments and flip-flop primitives, with no procedural blocks in the hardware design.
approach: I separated pixel timing from frame-based movement and composed collision handling, membrane controls, randomized motion, a timer and win/lose state logic.

When every molecule appeared at the origin, I traced the failure to reset ending before the derived clock began. FDRE initialization parameters established the intended positions at configuration time.
I used behavioral simulation stubs, focused timing and game-logic tests, and bitmap rendering to check both the logic and the actual visible output.
result: The provided display testbench completed two frames with zero sync errors and zero RGB-blanking errors.
Implemented eight moving molecules, color-selective membrane control and randomized positions, speeds and directions.
note: The animated card is a visual interpretation of the game, not a recording of the FPGA output.
technical: Pixel counters produce display coordinates and blanking signals; frame pulses advance object motion. Separating these time scales keeps collision and game-state updates independent of pixel traversal.

Configuration-time FDRE INIT values solve a different problem from synchronous runtime reset. The start-position failure required checking the clock-start sequence and rendered pixels, not just the state-machine transitions.

implementation.use: Compose game state and movement from structural logic.
Drive pixel coordinates, blanking and color output.
Check display timing and visible object positions.

title: HTTP / HTTPS proxy
headline: Making repeat requests work less.
summary: Concurrent request handling, bounded caching and encrypted traffic forwarding.
label: lower cached response time
problem: Repeated HTTP requests can duplicate origin work, while concurrent clients introduce shared-state hazards. I built a proxy to explore both response reuse and the correctness of network handling.
approach: I implemented FIFO and LRU eviction with a shared cache, keyed by the requested resource. Cache updates are synchronized, and incomplete or oversized responses are excluded.
The documented detached-thread variant uses POSIX threads for clients and CONNECT tunneling for HTTPS, relaying encrypted bytes without terminating the client’s TLS session.
A separate thread-pool variant explored bounded work queues and clean shutdown. I keep those designs distinct when discussing their concurrency behavior.
result: Reduced cached response time by 50% in the benchmark reported on my resume.
Built HTTP response caching with a 1 MB per-response bound and HTTPS CONNECT forwarding.
The archived test record reports argument validation, cache-policy sequences, response-body checks, sanitizer runs and concurrent-request exercises.
note: The 50% result applies to the cached-response benchmark reported on my resume; it is not a universal speedup across uncached requests or HTTPS tunnels.
technical: A cache entry is reusable only when the full HTTP response is available and within the size bound. A mutex protects shared cache mutation; the linked-list order implements FIFO insertion order or LRU recency.
HTTPS CONNECT is a bidirectional byte tunnel in the documented variant. TLS remains between client and origin, so the proxy cannot treat the encrypted payload as an ordinary cacheable HTTP response.

implementation.use: Parse HTTP requests and relay client/origin traffic.
Protect shared entries and manage eviction order.
Forward encrypted traffic as a bidirectional byte tunnel.

title: Gemma anomaly review
headline: From panel alerts to one incident.
summary: A separate language-model layer that makes energy anomalies easier to review.
label: one shared anomaly adapter
problem: Individual electrical panels can produce related anomaly signals. The aim was to turn those signals into one reviewable incident without changing the existing appliance-inference service.
approach: I built three logical panel agents around one Gemma adapter conditioned on panel identity. Their outputs are coordinated into a shared incident for review.
QLoRA with Hugging Face PEFT and TRL supported fine-tuning on Lambda GPUs; vLLM served the model. Respan captured traces and Nango connected a Google Sheets review workflow.
With only two verification rows in the anomaly table, I bootstrapped training labels by replaying the rule engine over archived readings.
result: Completed a hackathon prototype with model serving, traceability and a human review path.
Kept the anomaly layer separate from the BiLSTM / ONNX production inference path.
note: Completed refers to the prototype. Independent anomaly-detection accuracy and production alert outcomes are not established.
technical: Panel identity conditions a shared adapter rather than requiring three separately fine-tuned models. The incident coordinator combines those panel-level outputs into one reviewable event.
QLoRA reduces the fine-tuning memory requirement; vLLM handles serving. Respan traces and the Sheets review workflow expose model behavior, but do not by themselves establish anomaly accuracy.

implementation.use: Fine-tune one shared adapter conditioned on panel identity.
Serve the model for the three panel agents.
Trace outputs and connect incidents to a Sheets review workflow.

title: Tesphase
headline: Customer needs, translated into software.
summary: A mobile product exploring better use of household solar without additional customer hardware.
label: customer-discovery interviews
problem: Solar homeowners needed an approachable way to coordinate their energy use. At Tesphase, my role as CTO was to connect customer needs with a practical product roadmap and working application.
approach: I used more than 30 customer interviews to understand the workflows worth building first, then translated those findings into engineering priorities.
React Native provided the mobile interface, Supabase supported authentication and real-time data, and Node.js supported backend workflows. I owned the roadmap and architecture.
result: Shipped authentication, real-time database synchronization and push notifications.
Tesphase won SC Launchpad 2025. My CTO role ran from April through September 2025.
note: Proposed bill savings in the early lean canvas were product hypotheses, not measured customer outcomes.
technical: Authentication establishes the user identity used by application data. Real-time synchronization and push notifications serve different paths: updating shared state in the app versus drawing attention to an event. Product interviews informed which workflows received engineering effort first.

implementation.use: Build the mobile interface around customer priorities.
Support authentication and synchronized application data.
Connect backend workflows to the product roadmap.

title: Slug Board
headline: A clearer path into campus life.
summary: Event creation and participation workflows for UCSC students.
label: events, RSVPs and comments
problem: Campus activities are easy to miss when information stays inside separate college communities. Our team built Slug Board to bring event discovery and participation together.
approach: I owned event CRUD, the SQL schema and backend interaction logic for RSVPs, upvotes and comments.
I consolidated authentication, event and profile lookups in application code around a shared Profiles model during the move to React and Supabase.
As Sprint 2 Scrum Master, I helped coordinate the stack migration alongside feature delivery.
result: Implemented event CRUD, SQL updates and event-card interaction work as part of the team project.
The course retrospective records an incomplete MVP and significant backend integration failures. The project is marked completed as coursework, not as a fully delivered production service.
note: The archived reflection reports a 37.5% team completion rate for the MVP stage. It documents the learning and integration failures rather than a successful product launch.
technical: The retrospective identifies the critical integration boundary: event-card interactions depended on authentication, API behavior and database queries that were not consistently verified together.

The corrective approach is to validate endpoints and database contracts before wiring the interface, integrate across user stories earlier, and keep local branches synchronized. These are lessons from the retrospective, not claims of a subsequently rebuilt MVP.

implementation.use: Build event cards and participation interactions.
Model profiles, events, RSVPs, votes and comments.
Coordinate the stack migration and feature work across the team.

title: HTTP server on FPGA
headline: Taking a server into hardware.
summary: Exploring request handling and buffering beyond the software implementation.
label: software as a behavioral reference
problem: This project connects two areas of my work: network programming in C and synchronous digital design.
approach: I use the software server as a reference while exploring how request handling, buffering and board bring-up translate into FPGA hardware.
The work considers the Spartan-3E, Basys3 and Alchitry hardware mentioned in my project record.
result: The current outcome is a porting and bring-up effort.
The next milestone is an end-to-end HTTP request served on hardware.
note: A working hardware server and hardware performance figures are not yet established.
technical: The software server provides reference behavior for request parsing and responses. Buffering, state sequencing and the hardware network interface remain design constraints to resolve before an end-to-end board demonstration.

implementation.use: Use software request behavior as the porting reference.
Explore buffering and synchronous request-handling logic.
Work toward an end-to-end hardware request; this milestone remains open.

title: Two-player Quick Add
headline: Fair rounds. Correct scores.
summary: A two-player arithmetic game with synchronized inputs and explicit round control.
label: round and score controller
problem: Expanding a single-player game requires a shared response window, independent player state and correct handling of simultaneous inputs.
approach: I used synchronized and latched button inputs so both players could answer in the same round.
I traced a one-cycle mismatch between score updates and game-over detection, then added the missing transitions that prevented an extra round at zero points.
result: Both recorded testbenches passed after the fix, including ties, simultaneous wrong answers, no-response rounds and game-over lockout.
note: The project demonstrates structural control logic and focused verification.
technical: Two-flop synchronizers bring button signals into the clock domain; round latches retain each player’s response. The one-hot FSM resolves the shared window into scoring and the next round.

The score register and game controller observe values on clock boundaries. Explicit game-over transitions handle the updated score on the following cycle rather than assuming it is immediately visible.

implementation.use: Implement round control and registered score state.
Capture each player’s answer within a shared response window.
Check ties, missed answers and game-over transitions.

title: Quick Decode & counter lab
headline: From counters to reaction games.
summary: A progression from a 16-bit counter to a structurally designed reaction game.
label: loadable up/down counter
problem: Digital logic coursework moved from a stateful counter and display to reaction games with explicit sequencing.
approach: I built a 16-bit loadable up/down counter with seven-segment display output.
Quick Decode and Quick Add extended that foundation with one-hot state machines and LFSR-based logic under structural design constraints.

Earlier labs built an 8-bit ripple-carry adder/subtractor, two’s-complement sign changer, multiplexers and hexadecimal seven-segment decoding. Those components supplied the arithmetic and display foundation for the counter and games.
result: Completed the counter and reaction-game labs, building the synchronous design foundation used later in the Osmosis VGA game.
note: Coursework progression; no hardware performance benchmark is claimed.
technical: The counter lab exercises registered state, direction and load control. The reaction games add state sequencing and pseudo-random behavior; Osmosis extends the progression into display timing and moving objects.

implementation.use: Build loadable counters, arithmetic logic and registered state.
Display counter values and game output.
Add pseudo-random behavior and reaction-game sequencing.

title: Spiking neural networks
headline: Understanding why neurons stop learning.
summary: Experiments in spike encoding, normalization and trainable neuron dynamics.
label: encoding and training stability
problem: In Professor Eshraghian’s Neuromorphic Computing Group at UCSC, I explore how spiking networks preserve useful activity across time while supporting gradient-based learning. Several experiments stalled even when their architectures appeared plausible.
approach: On MNIST and CIFAR-10, I compared rate, Poisson and latency encodings, investigated threshold-dependent batch normalization and tuned membrane decay, firing thresholds and timesteps.
Layer activity, membrane behavior and loss traces helped separate dead neurons from optimizer and normalization failures.
A separate UCF101 prototype combined frozen ResNet18 features with a small spiking classifier. It remains a demonstration with a split-validation concern.
result: Built training pipelines and documented failure modes across multiple network configurations.
Moving experiments to Colab Pro reduced reported epoch time from about seven minutes to under two.
note: No validated accuracy or energy-efficiency advantage over a conventional CNN is claimed.
technical: Spike encoding maps image intensity into temporal events. LIF neurons integrate current with membrane decay and emit spikes at a threshold; surrogate gradients approximate the non-differentiable threshold during training.

Spike-health traces, loss behavior and optimizer updates must be checked together. Active neurons alone did not guarantee learning, while normalization changes could leave initialized currents too weak to cross threshold.

implementation.use: Train spiking models and inspect membrane and firing behavior.
Compare rate, Poisson and latency encoding experiments.
Run training and examine loss and spike-health traces.

title: ESP32 Weather Station in Rust
headline: From a sensor to a server.
summary: An ESP32-C3 client and Raspberry Pi service for collecting local and outdoor readings.
label: device-to-server workflow
problem: A small connected device needs to obtain configuration, gather sensor data and report readings to a service reliably.
approach: The ESP32-C3 fetches the server’s location, queries an outdoor-weather service and reads its onboard sensor.
The Raspberry Pi serves location data and accepts posted readings, separating device acquisition from server-side logging.
result: Implemented the coursework device/server workflow described in the October record; embedded coursework is ongoing.
note: The onboard sensor reading should not be presented as a calibrated ambient-temperature measurement.
technical: The device obtains location from GET /location and posts its readings to the Raspberry Pi service. Separating configuration, acquisition and reporting makes the device/server protocol explicit.

implementation.use: Implement the ESP32-C3 acquisition and reporting client.
Fetch location, query outdoor weather and post readings.
Provide location configuration and accept device data.

title: Battle Boats
headline: A game driven by interrupts.
summary: Battleship-style logic on a PIC32MX microcontroller.
label: event-driven embedded control
problem: A microcontroller game needs to respond to hardware events while keeping game state consistent.
approach: I organized Battleship-style gameplay as state machines and used timers, hardware interrupts and low-level peripheral drivers to connect software behavior to the board.
The archived implementation connects an Agent state machine to message parsing, negotiation, field state and OLED rendering. UART and circular-buffer modules carry the board-to-board message path.
result: Implemented the embedded game described in the project record, building experience with event-driven C and hardware interfaces.
note: No measured latency or performance benchmark is claimed.
technical: Timers and hardware interrupts supply events to the game state machines. Peripheral access and application state need clear boundaries so a hardware event produces one consistent state transition.

Separating negotiation, field updates and message events makes turn-taking explicit. The agent owns the transition between negotiation, attack, wait and end-game behavior while the display reflects that state.

implementation.use: Organize game behavior into an agent state machine.
Carry messages between boards.
Connect hardware events to gameplay and display state.

title: Concurrent HTTP file server
headline: Serving files without losing consistency.
summary: A C server connecting HTTP parsing, file operations, worker threads and request logging.
label: parsing, files and concurrency
problem: Concurrent clients can read and overwrite the same file. A server needs to parse partial network input correctly and coordinate file access so its responses and audit log tell a consistent story.
approach: I developed the server from a single-connection GET / PUT implementation into a concurrent design. The work covered request-line validation, header parsing, content lengths, response codes and cleanup of sockets and file descriptors.

I worked through worker dispatch, per-resource reader–writer locking and serialized audit logging. Debugging crossed several boundaries: listener APIs, partial reads, malformed requests and differences between local and submission builds.
result: Implemented the HTTP file-server coursework and documented the progression from protocol parsing to concurrent request handling.
The software work also provides the behavioral starting point for my separate FPGA HTTP experiment.
note: Completed describes the coursework implementation. The archive includes unresolved build and parsing iterations; it does not establish a production deployment or a throughput benchmark.
technical: A successful socket read can return only part of a request. The parser must preserve bytes already received after the header terminator and account for the remaining body before completing a PUT.
File locking and audit ordering are separate correctness concerns. Protecting file contents does not automatically make the log reflect the same operation order.

implementation.use: Handle partial requests, GET / PUT operations and responses.
Dispatch clients and coordinate shared-file access.
Work through build failures and protocol behavior.

title: Thread-safe queue & reader–writer locks
headline: Making shared state predictable.
summary: A bounded work queue and configurable reader–writer lock built with POSIX synchronization primitives.
label: reader, writer and bounded-reader modes
problem: Producers and consumers need to exchange work without racing, while shared resources need a clear rule for admitting readers and writers.
approach: I implemented a circular queue with head, tail and occupancy state guarded by a mutex. Separate condition variables represent available items and available capacity.
I implemented reader-preference, writer-preference and bounded-reader lock modes, tracking active and waiting participants to make admission policy explicit.
result: Built reusable queue and lock modules for the concurrent-systems coursework.
Made the tradeoff between throughput and waiting behavior a configurable part of the lock design.
note: The archive contains implementation and debugging work; it does not provide a verified starvation-freedom or stress-test result.
technical: Waiters recheck their predicates while holding the mutex after waking. A signal announces that state may have changed; it does not reserve an item or grant a lock.
An N-way policy limits reader admission when a writer is waiting. Correctness depends on maintaining the counters and wake-up conditions together.

implementation.use: Track head, tail and occupancy in a bounded queue.
Protect state and coordinate waiting producers and consumers.
Implement reader, writer and bounded-reader admission policies.

title: Command-driven file I/O
headline: Turning byte streams into file operations.
summary: A command-line get / set utility built around Unix file descriptors and explicit input validation.
label: command protocol over standard input
problem: A small file utility still has to distinguish command metadata from payload bytes, handle failed system calls and avoid assuming that one read or write transfers everything.
approach: I worked on a memory.c utility that reads get and set commands from standard input and maps them to file reads or replacements.
The implementation and review covered command parsing, declared payload length, file-opening flags, error messages and releasing allocated buffers and descriptors.
result: Built the file-I/O coursework foundation used later in HTTP request handling.
The project made byte counts, input boundaries and cleanup explicit parts of the interface.
note: Coursework implementation; the archived iterations do not establish a complete binary-data or large-file correctness suite.
technical: Text tokenization is appropriate for command fields, but payloads require byte-counted handling. The review exposed why treating the whole input as a null-terminated string is fragile.

implementation.use: Map get / set commands to file-descriptor operations.
Separate command fields from declared payload bytes.
Build and debug the command-line utility.

title: Pac-Man search agents
headline: Choosing a move by looking ahead.
summary: Reflex and adversarial agents that balance food collection, ghost avoidance and search depth.
label: state evaluation and action selection
problem: Greedy movement can trap an agent near food or a ghost. Planning requires a consistent model of turns, terminal states and the consequences of an action.
approach: I worked on reflex evaluation and adversarial search agents, using food distance, ghost proximity and scared timers to score successor states.
I debugged state-versus-position mistakes, repeated movement and depth handling, then ran repeated games without graphics to inspect outcomes across layouts.
result: Produced runnable agents and recorded wins, losses and scores during coursework experiments.
The experiments exposed how strongly performance depends on the layout, evaluator and depth setting.
note: The recorded runs use different configurations. I do not present a single selected win rate as a general benchmark.
technical: Minimax assumes an adversarial opponent; expectimax models chance. Alpha–beta pruning reduces unnecessary search while preserving the minimax decision for the same tree and evaluator.

implementation.use: Generate successor states and run repeated games.
Choose moves under adversarial assumptions and prune search.
Explore chance-based opponents and score food/ghost tradeoffs.

title: Gridworld & Pac-Man reinforcement learning
headline: Learning a policy from experience.
summary: Value iteration and Q-learning experiments on the exploration–exploitation tradeoff.
label: learning action values from rewards
problem: A useful action may require exploring a risky route before its reward is known. The challenge is to learn from experience while keeping training behavior separate from evaluation.
approach: I implemented action-value updates and epsilon-greedy selection, working through unseen state-action values, terminal states and ties between legal actions.
I used Gridworld and Pac-Man exercises to examine how learning rate, discounting and exploration affect the policy, including the BridgeGrid scenario and feature-based value approximation.
result: Built and debugged the learning-agent coursework and compared sampled learning with model-based value iteration.
The work made exploration settings and training versus test episodes explicit experimental choices.
note: No transferable win-rate or sample-efficiency improvement is claimed from the archived coursework.
technical: The Q update moves the current estimate toward reward plus the discounted best next-state value. A terminal transition has no future action value; handling that case prevents invalid action lookups.

implementation.use: Run Gridworld and Pac-Man learning exercises.
Update action values from observed transitions and rewards.
Compare exploration-based learning with model-based planning.

title: Capture-the-flag agents
headline: Knowing when to attack and when to defend.
summary: Cooperative Pac-Man agents with role switching, spatial features and trap-avoidance heuristics.
label: context-dependent agent behavior
problem: Two agents must collect food, protect home territory and avoid interfering with each other. A fixed offensive or defensive role cannot respond to every board state.
approach: I developed weighted features for food, capsules, visible opponents, teammate distance and return behavior. The policy switches between attack and defense as threats change.
I investigated stop/reverse penalties, narrow corridors and corner traps, and adjusted distance-based behavior when excessive avoidance caused agents to oscillate.
result: Implemented a team-agent policy and wrote a technical retrospective explaining its representation, decision rules and limitations.
The result is a concrete study of coordination under competing objectives.
note: The archive supports implementation and report work, but does not establish a tournament placement or a controlled improvement over a baseline.
technical: Maze distance captures walls that Manhattan distance ignores. Feature weights still need care: rewarding distance from a teammate or opponent too strongly can overpower the goal of making progress.

implementation.use: Implement a cooperative capture-the-flag policy.
Measure routes around walls to food, allies and threats.
Switch between attack and defense and penalize traps or reversal.

title: AVL word-range index
headline: Counting a range without scanning every word.
summary: An augmented AVL tree for insertions and lexicographic range-count queries.
label: subtree sizes alongside balance metadata
problem: A word index needs to accept insertions while answering how many entries lie between two keys. An unbalanced tree or a full traversal makes those queries unnecessarily expensive.
approach: I worked on an AVL tree that stores both height and subtree size, with rotations maintaining balance and the metadata needed for rank queries.
I traced zero and negative range counts through size updates, rotation order and comparisons, distinguishing numeric-looking strings from the assignment’s lexicographic keys.
result: Implemented the indexed-query coursework and investigated failures with explicit insertion sequences and expected range counts.
The intended design answers a range count using two rank traversals rather than enumerating every matching node.
note: Logarithmic query complexity is a property of the correctly maintained AVL design, not a measured speedup. The archive includes debugging cases without a final comprehensive pass report.
technical: For inclusive bounds, count(keys ≤ upper) − count(keys < lower) handles the boundary correctly. Heights and sizes must be recomputed after rotations in child-before-parent order.

implementation.use: Maintain a balanced index as words are inserted.
Compute inclusive range counts from two rank traversals.
Trace incorrect counts through height, size and comparison updates.

title: Six Degrees: actor connection finder
headline: Finding the shortest story between two actors.
summary: An actor–movie graph that returns a shortest connection with the films that explain every step.
label: shortest paths with movie provenance
problem: A connection finder needs to return more than a distance: the user should see which shared films connect the actors.
approach: I parsed cast lists, mapped actor and movie names to integer IDs and stored movie IDs with actor-to-actor edges.
Breadth-first search tracks visited actors and records both the previous actor and the film used to reach each node. I reconstruct the path from that parent map.
result: Built a file-driven graph query program that expresses the connection as an actor-and-film chain.
Worked through parsing, disconnected inputs and path reconstruction rather than treating traversal alone as the finished feature.
note: The archived implementation uses pairwise cast connections; a movie with a large cast can create many edges. No large-dataset performance claim is made.
technical: BFS finds a shortest path by edge count in an unweighted graph. Keeping movie identity on the predecessor edge preserves an explanation of why each connection exists.

implementation.use: Map actor and movie names to compact IDs.
Find the fewest actor-to-actor connections.
Recover both the actors and films explaining the path.

title: Data structures & constraint-solving lab
headline: Making the algorithm visible in the data structure.
summary: A collection of linked-list, graph, word-analysis and backtracking implementations.
label: from memory ownership to search
problem: High-level containers hide the state changes that make an algorithm work. These exercises made memory ownership, traversal state and constraints explicit.
approach: I built linked-list and graph ADTs, indirect lexicographic sorting, a deck-shuffle client and a Shakespeare word-frequency index grouped by word length.

I worked on N-Queens with preset placements and an explicit search stack, alongside stack-based anagram generation and smaller simulation exercises. Debugging focused on preserving fixed constraints while undoing only speculative choices.
result: Created a set of command-line coursework programs with file-based inputs and outputs.
The N-Queens history includes a user-confirmed working version after a valid preset board had incorrectly returned “No solution.”
note: These are educational implementations, grouped here rather than presented as separate production products.
technical: An explicit stack must retain enough state to resume a search after backtracking. A linked-list cursor must distinguish being off-list from pointing at a valid node; that invariant affects insertion and deletion alike.

implementation.use: Build ADTs, word indexes and indirect sorting clients.
Represent connections and explore reachable states.
Resume constraint search while preserving fixed N-Queens placements.

title: Virtual network topology lab
headline: Debugging a network before buying hardware.
summary: A Mininet topology exercise connecting hosts, switches and traffic-controlled links.
label: repeatable network setup
problem: A network diagram does not show whether host interfaces, links and addressing behave as intended. Emulation makes those relationships inspectable.
approach: I worked through a Python topology representing user devices and home equipment connected through two switches.
I configured host/link definitions and used the Mininet environment to inspect interface state and distinguish host commands from the surrounding Linux shell.
result: Developed the virtual-network lab setup and an operational understanding of where network commands execute.
The topology provides a repeatable environment for exploring connectivity without a physical switch bench.
note: This is a topology and configuration exercise; the export does not establish a verified routing policy or measured throughput.
technical: Adding a link does not by itself solve addressing or routing. Host namespaces and switch connectivity need to be checked separately when diagnosing reachability.

implementation.use: Define virtual hosts, switches and links.
Configure link behavior for the topology exercise.
Inspect interfaces and distinguish host commands from the outer shell.

title: Saaf / Saaf Safai
headline: A simpler starting point for shared chores.
summary: Early interface and authentication work for a chore-and-reminder application.
label: mobile and web explorations
problem: Chore coordination starts with a low-friction entry into the application. Before building reminder logic, the interface and development environment need a reliable foundation.
approach: I explored a React Native welcome screen with a centered identity and message, then worked through simulator startup and Metro configuration.
A separate web exploration used Next.js and Supabase for the login path. The history includes dependency installation and project-structure debugging across the two approaches.
result: Established the app concept, welcome-screen work and authentication scaffold.
The next meaningful milestone is an integrated chore workflow with persistence and reminders.
note: The mobile and web experiments are distinct prototypes. Completed reminder scheduling, production authentication and an app release are not established.
technical: The archive’s failures occur before feature logic: obsolete CLI paths, missing Metro configuration and package setup. Resolving the toolchain is necessary before claiming an end-to-end product.

title: Analog circuits & filter characterization

problem: A transfer function predicts behavior, but a bench circuit adds loading, component tolerance and measurement choices. The task was to connect observed voltage and phase to the model.
approach: I worked through KCL/KVL, superposition and Thévenin/Norton equivalents, then analyzed capacitor and inductor transients using the single-time-constant model.
For sinusoidal filters, I used the supplied measurement data to build gain and phase tables and Bode plots, relating time delay to phase and comparing low-pass and high-pass behavior.
result: Produced lab analyses and reports spanning DC equivalents, transient behavior and frequency response.
The work connected amplitude and timing observations to the equations used to design filters.
note: These are coursework measurements and analyses. No component-accuracy or instrumentation-performance improvement is claimed.
technical: Magnitude is expressed as 20 log10(Vout/Vin). Phase follows from the time shift at the measurement frequency; both the sign convention and the distinction between peak and peak-to-peak values matter.
